title: Determinants of Effective Loose Dangerous Goods Management in Port Operations: Empirical Evidence From Port Klang, Malaysia
content:
Survey findings from 52 Port Klang stakeholders identify regulatory compliance, staff competency, standard operating procedures, and inter-agency coordination as significant positive predictors of perceived loose dangerous goods handling effectiveness. Infrastructure and technological support showed no statistically significant independent association, highlighting the importance of governance and operational practices.


ABSTRACT

Dangerous goods (DGs) in loose form are a major problem and challenge when it comes to handling at maritime ports because of the risk of leakage, contamination, and regulatory non-compliance. This is a study on the effectiveness of loose dangerous goods management practices at Port Klang, the port authority's main seaport in Malaysia, looking at the factors of dangerous goods regulatory adherence, staff training and competency, standard operating procedures (SOPs), infrastructure and technological support, and coordination between required agencies. Using a quantitative research approach, structured questionnaires were given to 52 stakeholders involved in the port operations, customs departments, marine departments, logistics service providers, freight forwarders, and safety personnel. The reliability of the research instrument was assessed using a pilot study with 30 respondents, with all constructs demonstrating acceptable internal consistency, with Cronbach's alpha values of at least 0.792. Data was analyzed using SPSS descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression analysis. Results indicated that regulatory compliance (β = 0.341 with p < 0.01), staff training and competency (β = 0.309 with p < 0.01), standard operating procedures (SOPs) (β = 0.260 with p < 0.05) and inter-agency co-ordination (β = 0.223 with p < 0.05) are the factors significantly influencing the effectiveness of loose dangerous goods handling; infrastructure and technological support were not shown to affect it statistically significantly. For regression, the variance of the handling effectiveness captured was 68.2%. The study adds to the ongoing sparse empirical research about loose dangerous goods management in Southeast Asian ports, and offers concrete suggestions on how to enhance the security of maritime transportation, regulation enforcement, and operational coordination for the handling of dangerous goods.
